outcome: No Wall–Sun–Sun prime has been found or excluded since 26 January 2024, and the existence question is still open; the in-window items are a 2025 reformulation (Ross, Shen and Cai), a 2026 generalisation to WSS(d) primes for quadratic fields (Shi et al.), and a self-published 2026 near-WSS note that claims no WSS prime; the only computational bound, a PrimeGrid search to 2^64, was reported as ending in late 2022 but I could not confirm its completion.
problem_asks: Single existence question: is there a prime p > 5 with p² dividing the Fibonacci number F_(p − (p/5)), where (p/5) is the Legendre symbol? Equivalent forms in the sources: p² | F_π(p) with π(p) the Pisano period (rank of apparition); or π(p²) = π(p); or F_(p−(5/p)) ≡ 0 (mod p²). A 'yes' answer needs one such prime; a 'no' answer needs a proof that none exists. Scope notes, not parts of the bullet: the bullet does not ask whether there are infinitely many such primes (Wikipedia calls the conjectured count infinite); it does not ask about the k-generalisations or (a,b)-generalisations (Jones and others) except where a result on those bears on the (1,1) case.

events.what_happened: D. D. Wall, 'Fibonacci Series Modulo m', American Mathematical Monthly 67 (1960) 525–532, asked whether a prime p can have π(p²) = π(p), i.e. p² | F_π(p). Wikipedia reports that Wall's computer test found no such prime below 10,000 and that the question was left open. I did not open the original; the characterisation comes from Wikipedia and from Sun's 1992 abstract.
events.delivers: Poses the question. Gives no existence or non-existence result. The computer check it reports covers only a small range (10,000 per Wikipedia).
events.direction: Neither way; it is the origin of the question.

events.what_happened: Zhi-Hong Sun and Zhi-Wei Sun, 'Fibonacci numbers and Fermat's last theorem', Acta Arithmetica 60 (1992) 371–388. The IMPAN record lists Zhi-Wei Sun as the sole author; Wikipedia and other sources name both Suns. The abstract, as read on the IMPAN page, says the affirmative answer to Wall's question implies the first case of Fermat's Last Theorem, and gives a new formula for the Fibonacci quotient F_(p−(5/p))/p.
events.delivers: A conditional link. If the first case of Fermat's Last Theorem fails at an odd prime exponent p, then p is a Wall–Sun–Sun prime. In the abstract's wording, the affirmative answer to Wall's question (read by the search summary as 'p² never divides F_(p−(5/p))') implies the first case of FLT. No existence or non-existence result for WSS primes.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. FLT itself was proved by Wiles and Taylor in 1995, so the link is now historical rather than a route to a counterexample.

checked_by.who: Acta Arithmetica (Polish Academy of Sciences, IMPAN)

events.direction: Ties the problem to FLT. Cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: A 2004 search by R. J. McIntosh, reported only as a MathWorld citation ('McIntosh, R. Email to Paul Zimmermann, 9 Mar 2004'), states that there are no Wall–Sun–Sun primes up to 10^14. It is not a public paper and I did not read it. MathWorld is the only source I have for it.
events.delivers: No WSS prime below 10^14, as a computer negative. Says nothing about primes above 10^14.
events.doubts: Known only through MathWorld's citation to a private email; the search is not described in any public text I could read. Elsenhans and Jahnel (2010) report the same 10^14 range independently.
events.direction: Computational negative below 10^14. Cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: R. J. McIntosh and E. L. Roettger, 'A search for Fibonacci–Wieferich and Wolstenholme primes', Mathematics of Computation 76 (2007), no. 260, 2087–2094. Per a search snippet (the AMS page returned HTTP 403 and I did not open it), the paper finds no Fibonacci–Wieferich primes below 2×10^14. Wikipedia gives the same bound: 'if any exist, they must be > 2×10^14'.
events.delivers: No WSS prime below 2×10^14, as a computer negative.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper; the computation was not re-run

events.directly_checkable: Any putative example p is checkable by computing F_(p−(p/5)) modulo p² with modular Fibonacci arithmetic. No hit has been reported in this range.
events.doubts: The bound is taken from a search snippet and Wikipedia, not from the paper itself, which I could not open.
events.direction: Computational negative below 2×10^14.

events.what_happened: Zhi-Hong Sun, 'Fibonacci numbers modulo cubes of primes', arXiv:0911.3060 (later Taiwanese Journal of Mathematics 17 (2013)). Per a search snippet, the paper determines F_(p−(p/5)) modulo p³ from a central binomial coefficient sum and poses conjectures. I did not open the arXiv page.
events.revisions: Journal version Taiwanese J. Math. 17 (2013) per search snippet.
events.delivers: A finer congruence for the Fibonacci quotient at p − (p/5). Nothing on existence of WSS primes.
events.doubts: Not opened; the description comes from a search snippet.
events.direction: Neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: A.-S. Elsenhans and J. Jahnel, 'The Fibonacci sequence modulo p² – an investigation by computer for p < 10^14', arXiv:1006.0824, first submitted 4 June 2010. Abstract as read: for primes p < 10^14, the period length κ(p²) of the Fibonacci sequence mod p² is never equal to its period length mod p; the same range gives κ(p^n) = κ(p)·p^(n−1). Journal publication not confirmed.
events.delivers: No WSS prime p < 10^14, by computer (the condition π(p²) = π(p) fails for every prime in range). Also the general formula κ(p^n) = κ(p)·p^(n−1) for primes below 10^14. Nothing for p ≥ 10^14.
events.doubts: Computer search with no independent re-run found. Wikipedia cites this paper for the 10^14 check. A later search summary, not verified by me, attributes it to a 2014 scan; the arXiv record is 2010.
events.direction: Negative below 10^14. Consistent with WSS primes not existing in range; cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: F. G. Dorais and D. W. Klyve, 'A Wieferich prime search up to 6.7×10^15', Journal of Integer Sequences 14 (2011), Article 11.9.2 (received 30 June 2011; published 16 October 2011). Abstract as read: no Wieferich primes below 6.7×10^15 beyond 1093 and 3511; the same methods extend the search for Fibonacci–Wieferich primes, concluding there are none below 9.7×10^14. The date is the journal publication, since I found no earlier public version.
events.delivers: No WSS (Fibonacci–Wieferich) prime p < 9.7×10^14, by computer. The Wieferich result is a different question and is not counted here.
events.direction: Negative below 9.7×10^14. Cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: Arpan Saha and C. S. Karthik, 'A Few Equivalences of Wall–Sun–Sun Prime Conjecture', arXiv:1102.1636, first submitted 8 February 2011 (v2 14 March 2011). Abstract as read: proves lemmas on Fibonacci numbers mod primes, gives several statements equivalent to the conjecture, offers heuristics, and proposes further conjectures. It does not claim to decide existence.
events.delivers: Equivalent reformulations and heuristics only. No existence or non-existence result.
events.direction: Neither way. Reformulations and heuristics.

events.what_happened: George Grell and Wayne Peng, 'Wall's Conjecture and the ABC Conjecture', arXiv:1511.01210, first submitted 4 November 2015. Abstract as read: assuming the abc conjecture for number fields, there are infinitely many non-Fibonacci–Wieferich primes (primes with π(p²) ≠ π(p)), with a heuristic count below a given value.
events.delivers: Conditional on the number-field abc conjecture: infinitely many primes that are NOT WSS. This concerns the complement of the WSS set, so it does not decide whether any WSS prime exists.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: existence of at least one WSS prime.
events.doubts: Conditional on an unproven conjecture (abc over number fields). The reduction to Wall's conjecture is from the abstract as read.
events.direction: Conditional result about non-WSS primes. Cuts neither way on whether WSS primes exist.

events.what_happened: Wayne Peng, 'ABC implies there are infinitely many non-Fibonacci–Wieferich primes – an application of ABC conjecture over number fields', arXiv:1511.05645, posted November 2015 (per search snippet). Published in Journal of Number Theory 212 (2020) 354–375 (per search snippet). Generalises to X-base Fibonacci–Wieferich primes for a finite set X of algebraic numbers. I did not open the arXiv page.
events.revisions: Journal version J. Number Theory 212 (2020) 354–375 per search snippet.
events.delivers: Conditional on abc over number fields: infinitely many primes that are not X-base Fibonacci–Wieferich. Concerns the complement of the WSS set; no existence result for WSS primes.

checked_by.qualification: Refereed journal of record (per search snippet)
checked_by.what_they_did: Published the paper in 2020 (per search snippet)

events.doubts: Conditional on an unproven conjecture. Not opened; description from search snippets.
events.direction: Conditional, about non-WSS primes. Cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's PRPNet 'Wall–Sun–Sun Prime Search', per MathWorld, extended the search in November 2015 to 1.4597479×10^17. I did not open the PRPNet page. A search summary of a PrimeGrid forum thread reported a previous PRPNet endpoint of 2.6438336×10^17; I could not verify that figure.
events.revisions: Superseded in scope by the 2020–2022 joint Wieferich/WSS search (see primegrid-ww-2022).
events.delivers: No WSS prime below 1.4597479×10^17, by computer, as cited by MathWorld.
events.doubts: Only known via MathWorld. The PRPNet page and the forum thread were not read.
events.direction: Computational negative below 1.46×10^17. Cuts neither way on existence.
people: PrimeGrid volunteers (not named in the sources read)

events.what_happened: Nicholas Bragman and Eric Rowland, 'Limiting density of the Fibonacci sequence modulo powers of a prime', arXiv:2202.00704, first submitted 1 February 2022; revised 23 August 2025. Abstract as read: determines the limiting density, as λ → ∞, of residues mod p^λ attained by the Fibonacci sequence; relates it to zeros of Lucas numbers mod p; the proof uses 'a characterization of Wall–Sun–Sun primes p in terms of the p-adic absolute value'.
events.revisions: v1 1 Feb 2022; v2 23 Aug 2025 (content of v2 not read).
events.delivers: A p-adic reformulation of WSS used in a density computation. No existence result for WSS primes.
events.direction: Reformulation. Cuts neither way.

events.what_happened: Lenny Jones, 'A Connection Between the Monogenicity of Certain Power-Compositional Trinomials and k-Wall–Sun–Sun Primes', arXiv:2211.14834, late 2022 (exact date not read). Per a search snippet: f(x^(s^n)) is monogenic for all n ≥ 1 iff no prime divisor of s is a k-WSS prime, under stated hypotheses. Not opened.
events.delivers: A monogenicity equivalence for trinomials, conditional on hypotheses on s. No existence result for WSS primes.
events.doubts: Not opened; description from a search snippet.
events.direction: Neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: PrimeGrid's joint Wieferich and Wall–Sun–Sun search (WWocl application). Per Wikipedia it began in November 2020. A forum test thread of 30 December 2020 (thread 9508) reports the app's software limit raised from 2^62 to 2^64. The end-of-project notice (thread 10037) was posted 14 November 2022; an update of 20 November 2022 gave a leading edge of 17660.716P (about 1.766×10^19, about 95.7% complete) and 19–27 days remaining. Wikipedia says the project ended in December 2022 and that 'any such prime must exceed 2^64' (about 1.8×10^19); the 2023 Jones paper repeats this bound, citing Wikipedia. I found no closing results post. The visible thread reports no WSS prime and says results were still being counted.
events.revisions: Project start Nov 2020 (Wikipedia); software limit raised to 2^64 by 30 Dec 2020 (thread 9508); end notice 14 Nov 2022 (thread 10037); the 20 Nov update gives 95.7% complete.
events.delivers: If complete and correct, no WSS prime p < 2^64 (about 1.8×10^19). That is a computer negative over finitely many p. It says nothing about a WSS prime above 2^64, so it does not decide existence. Completion is not confirmed.
events.remains: Every WSS prime above 2^64, which is all of problem_asks as a question about existence.

checked_by.who: PrimeGrid forum testers and staff (individuals not named in the thread text I read)
checked_by.qualification: Volunteer project staff and testers; not mathematicians reviewing the result
checked_by.what_they_did: Ran test ranges and reported checksums on the app version (thread 9508); posted the end-of-project notice (thread 10037)

events.directly_checkable: A counterexample is a prime p < 2^64 with p² dividing F_(p−(p/5)). Checkable by modular Fibonacci arithmetic; the search reports none.
events.doubts: The 2^64 claim rests on a project whose last reported state I read (20 Nov 2022) was about 95.7% complete with 19–27 days left. I found no closing post or independent re-run confirming it finished. The Jones 2023 bound and the Wikipedia statement cite each other, so the bound is not an independent check.
events.direction: Computer negative below 2^64, if complete. Cuts neither way on existence.
people: Reggie (PrimeGrid, named as announcer in thread 9508)

events.what_happened: Lenny Jones, 'Generalized Wall–Sun–Sun primes and monogenic power-compositional trinomials', arXiv:2301.05566, first submitted 13 January 2023; latest version v6 19 February 2023. Abstract as read: defines an (a,b)-Wall–Sun–Sun prime as a prime p with gcd(p,b) = 1 and π(p²) = π(p) for the Lucas sequence with parameters (a,b); shows monogenicity of f(x^(s^n)) is independent of n and depends on whether s has an (a,b)-WSS prime divisor. An arXiv administrator note records substantial text overlap with arXiv:2211.14834.
events.revisions: v1 13 Jan 2023; v2 16 Jan; v3 18 Jan; v4 28 Jan; v5 10 Feb; v6 19 Feb 2023.
events.delivers: Generalises WSS primes to (a,b) Lucas sequences. For (a,b) = (1,1), which is the Fibonacci case, it uses the same definition and gives no existence result.
events.remains: Existence of a (1,1) WSS prime (all of problem_asks), and existence for all (a,b).
events.doubts: The arXiv admin note flags substantial text overlap with arXiv:2211.14834 (as read on the abstract page). Not a review finding.
events.direction: Generalisation. Cuts neither way on the (1,1) existence question.

events.what_happened: Joshua Harrington and Lenny Jones, 'A note on generalised Wall–Sun–Sun primes', Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society, published online by Cambridge University Press 28 February 2023 (per search snippet; the Cambridge page was not opened). Gives necessary and sufficient conditions for a prime dividing a²+4b to be an (a,b)-WSS prime. No arXiv posting found.
events.delivers: Conditions for primes dividing a²+4b to be (a,b)-WSS. A generalisation; no existence result for the (1,1) case.
events.remains: All of problem_asks for the (1,1) case.

checked_by.who: Bulletin of the Australian Mathematical Society (Cambridge University Press)

events.doubts: Not opened; description from a search snippet.
events.direction: Generalisation. Cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: Lenny Jones, 'A New Condition for k-Wall–Sun–Sun Primes', arXiv:2302.10357, first submitted 20 February 2023 (v2 27 Feb; v3 16 Mar; v4 15 Jul 2023); published Taiwanese Journal of Mathematics 28(1) (February 2024), pp. 17–28, DOI 10.11650/tjm/231003. Main result: for k ≢ 0 (mod 4) with the discriminant squarefree, p is a k-WSS prime iff x^(2p) − kx^p − 1 is non-monogenic. For k = 1 this is the Fibonacci case. The paper also states, citing Crandall–Dilcher–Pomerance (1997) and Wikipedia (2023): 'as of December 2022, if p is a Wall–Sun–Sun prime, then p > 2^64', and 'The question of whether any Wall–Sun–Sun primes exist is still unresolved.'
events.revisions: v1 20 Feb 2023; v2 27 Feb 2023; v3 16 Mar 2023; v4 15 Jul 2023; journal version Taiwanese J. Math. 28(1) Feb 2024 (after the freeze; the arXiv date is used per the dating rule).
events.delivers: For k = 1, a monogenicity criterion equivalent to WSS. An equivalence, not a decision. It also records the 2^64 lower bound as of December 2022, cited to Wikipedia and to a 1997 paper.
events.remains: Existence of a k = 1 WSS prime (all of problem_asks). The criterion is an equivalence, so existence is unchanged.

checked_by.what_they_did: Accepted and published the paper, February 2024

events.doubts: The 2^64 bound is cited to Wikipedia, which cites the PrimeGrid search whose completion I could not confirm (see primegrid-ww-2022). Not a doubt about the theorem itself.
events.direction: Reformulation of the k = 1 case. Cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: Tyler Ross, Zhongyan Shen and Tianxin Cai, 'The p-adic Valuations of Möbius Duals of Lucas Sequences', arXiv:2512.03481, first submitted 3 December 2025. The abstract's last sentence says the valuations are related to the existence of WSS primes. Section 5 states 'there are no Wall–Sun–Sun primes smaller than 9.7×10^14', citing Dorais and Klyve (2011). Corollary 5.1 states that there are no WSS primes iff 'the numbers M_n^F are squarefree for all n ≠ 6' (as rendered on ar5iv).
events.revisions: v1 3 Dec 2025. No later version read.
events.delivers: A reformulation: non-existence of WSS primes is equivalent to squarefreeness of M_n^F for n ≠ 6. It restates the 2011 Dorais–Klyve bound. It establishes no existence or non-existence.
events.doubts: The corollary is a reformulation whose proof I did not read. The paper cites the 2011 bound 9.7×10^14, not the later 2^64 search, so its bound is out of date. Full text not read; only the abstract page and the ar5iv rendering.
events.direction: Equivalence. Cuts neither way on existence.

events.what_happened: Minjia Shi, Xuan Wang, Bouazzaoui Zakariae, Jon-Lark Kim and Patrick Solé, 'Second order Recurrences, quadratic number fields and cyclic codes', arXiv:2603.25343, submitted 26 March 2026 (v1 only as read). Abstract as read: defines WSS(d) primes for second-order recurrences tied to the principal unit of Q(√d), and studies weight distributions of cyclic codes over F_p and Z_{p²}, reporting MDS or NMDS codes. It does not claim a new WSS prime, and I found no computation or AI disclosure in the abstract or metadata.
events.delivers: A generalisation to WSS(d) for quadratic fields, with coding-theory results. Nothing on the existence of classical WSS primes.
events.doubts: Full text not read; only the abstract and metadata were available.
events.direction: Generalisation. Cuts neither way on the classical question.

events.what_happened: Nobuki Fujimoto (fc0web), 'Paper 104: Near Wall–Sun–Sun primes in Collatz peaks' (labelled 'Rei-AIOS Paper 104'), self-published and reposted on dev.to. The body says a full check of WSS primes for p ≤ 10,000 found none. It defines near-WSS as Fibonacci residue below 100 mod p², finds five such primes (3, 7, 11, 13, 19), four of which occur as Collatz-peak factors for n ≤ 50,000, and proposes a conjecture T-WC+ that it verifies empirically for those five primes. The paper explicitly does not claim any WSS prime was found. The author credits the paper as '(Rei-AIOS)' and states 'Three-party co-authorship per OUKC charter v1.0' in metadata, without naming the parties.
events.revisions: Draft dated 2026-04-16 ('78-day hold-back'); the dev.to metadata gives Jul 2 and the metadata line gives 'Published 2026-07-03'. The first public date is therefore early July 2026.
events.delivers: Nothing on WSS existence. It checks p ≤ 10,000 and reports a near-WSS analogue. The conjecture concerns Collatz peaks.
events.directly_checkable: The p ≤ 10,000 check is directly reproducible from the Fibonacci congruence; the paper does not give its code.
events.doubts: Self-published and not peer-reviewed; no independent verification found. A search summary, which I did not verify, reports that the T-WC+ criterion (residue < p) does not match the table's residues (21, 55, 39, 57, all larger than their primes), because the search uses residue < 100. The body cites a Paper 102 that I did not find. It cites an Elsenhans–Jahnel 2014 scan; the arXiv record is 2010.
events.direction: Not a WSS result. A near-WSS analogue and a Collatz conjecture. Cuts neither way on the classical question.

disputes.summary: Who first searched below 10^14 is given two ways: MathWorld credits McIntosh (2004 email) and Wikipedia credits the 10^14 check to Elsenhans and Jahnel (2010, arXiv). Both are negative computer searches in the same range, so this is an attribution question and not a dispute over a result.
The 1992 Acta Arithmetica paper is listed under Zhi-Wei Sun alone by the IMPAN record, and under both Zhi-Hong and Zhi-Wei Sun by Wikipedia and other sources.

The 2^64 bound (Jones 2023, citing Wikipedia; Wikipedia citing PrimeGrid) and the 9.7×10^14 bound (Ross, Shen and Cai 2025, citing Dorais–Klyve 2011) are both in circulation. The later, larger bound supersedes the earlier one; they are not contradictory.

summary: The question has no event in the window that moves its existence status. Across 39 web searches and about 30 page fetches, I found no WSS prime, no claimed counterexample and no claimed proof or disproof from 26 January 2024 to the present, and I found no AI system credited with anything on this problem. The record is mostly pre-window: Wall (1960) posed the question; Sun and Sun (1992) linked it to FLT; a series of computer searches ruled out ranges, first to 10^14 (McIntosh 2004 by MathWorld's citation; Elsenhans–Jahnel 2010), then to 2×10^14 (McIntosh–Roettger 2007), 9.7×10^14 (Dorais–Klyve 2011), 1.46×10^17 (PrimeGrid PRPNet 2015), and finally to 2^64 (PrimeGrid joint Wieferich/WSS search, end notice 14 November 2022). The 2^64 bound is the strongest, but I could not confirm that the search finished: the last state I read (20 November 2022) was 95.7% complete with 19–27 days remaining, and the bound 'p > 2^64' is repeated by Jones (2023) and Wikipedia, which cite each other. In-window items are restatements or generalisations: Ross, Shen and Cai (3 December 2025) reformulate non-existence as squarefreeness of M_n^F and restate the 2011 bound; Shi et al. (26 March 2026) study WSS(d) primes for quadratic fields with coding-theory results; Fujimoto (early July 2026, self-published) reports a near-WSS analogue in Collatz peaks and checks p ≤ 10,000, explicitly claiming no WSS prime. Bragman and Rowland's 2022 paper was revised in August 2025, but the revision is outside the scope of this question. Two judgement calls: first, I treat the 2^64 result as a computer negative with no bearing on existence above 2^64, as the existence question is not a question about the smallest prime. Second, I treat the Fujimoto paper as having an ambiguous AI involvement: it names 'Rei-AIOS' and 'three-party co-authorship' in its metadata, but the body never says what any system did, so I list no system. No source I opened names an AI system in connection with this problem. The AI search returned only unrelated items: Anthropic's unreleased-Claude paper on the Riemann-zeta zeros (August 2026, per Scientific American); Anthropic's Jacobian counterexample; OpenAI's unit-distance result (May 2026); Erdős problems; and a prime-gap Lean formalisation credited to 'GPT-6-Astra' by an aggregator and not verified. None concerns Wall–Sun–Sun primes. Epoch AI's FrontierMath: Open Problems page showed 10 of 49 problems; its keyword check found no Fibonacci, Wall or Wieferich, but I could not see the rest of the list.
competing_reading: A reader could treat the PrimeGrid search to 2^64 as a finished, strong computer negative, so that the problem is 'open but almost certainly false in any practical sense' and the problem's status is settled by a judgement that the answer is 'no WSS prime below 2^64'. Against that, the completion of that search is not confirmed by any closing post I could find, so the bound may be lower. A second reading takes the Sun–Sun 1992 link as a partial result: the affirmative answer to Wall's question implies FLT's first case. That is a conditional statement about the same object, but FLT is now proved, so it cannot move the existence question. The Ross et al. 2025 corollary might be read as a non-existence equivalence; its proof was not read, so this reading is unverified.
what_would_settle_it: For the search: a PrimeGrid closing or statistics page showing that the Wall–Sun–Sun range below 2^64 was fully covered, with no hit. For existence: either a prime p with p² dividing F_(p−(p/5)), which would be checkable by modular Fibonacci arithmetic, or a proof that none exists. For the in-window items: the full text of arXiv:2512.03481 Corollary 5.1, and whether the 2025 Ross–Shen–Cai reformulation or Shi et al. 2026 has been cited by anyone as a result on the classical question.

judgement.why: The statement is a single existence question. Every computer search (McIntosh, McIntosh–Roettger, Elsenhans–Jahnel, Dorais–Klyve, PrimeGrid) is a finite check with no hit, so these are instances, not bounds on an open quantity: the question is not about the size of the smallest WSS prime. Equivalent reformulations (Saha–Karthik, Bragman–Rowland, Jones k=1 criterion, Ross–Shen–Cai Corollary 5.1) and the Sun–Sun FLT link decide nothing and score none. Generalisations to (a,b), k, WSS(d) primes, and the abc-conditional results about non-WSS primes, answer changed questions and score variant. The Jones 2023 k-WSS paper was published in Feb 2024 but its arXiv date is Feb 2023, so it predates the snapshot. Fujimoto's paper has a vague 'Rei-AIOS' / three-party co-authorship mention but no system is recorded doing mathematics, and it settles only a near-WSS analogue, so ai_role none. No post-snapshot event moves the problem.
judgement.doubts: The 2^64 PrimeGrid bound's completion is unconfirmed; irrelevant to the outcome since finite searches are instances either way. Fujimoto's AI involvement is undisclosed in substance.
